sentences.t: Maruti Motors was incorporated in 1971 with Sanjay Gandhi, the prime minister's younger son, as its first managing director - a private company to design, build and assemble a small car for India, per Business Standard's history.
It never built one at scale.
After the 1977 change of government the venture collapsed; Forbes India's retelling records that the firm was dissolved that year.
The resurrection was a state act.
After Indira Gandhi returned to power, the government took over the undertaking and incorporated Maruti Udyog Limited in February 1981, per Forbes India's retelling.

The project carried its politics with it: Business Standard's history records that it was "deemed to be born in sin," amid charges of abuse of public policy, irregular land allocation and money laundering against the Gandhis.
What the state had inherited was a name, some land and a brief - build a people's car - with no car, no partner and no factory able to make one.
The search for a collaborator began there.
Suzuki was not India's first choice.

Renault, Volkswagen, MAN and Ford had all expressed interest, per Business Standard's history; talks proceeded furthest with Renault, until the numbers killed them - the Renault 18's 1,647 cc engine put the car at Rs 1.15 lakh on the road, import duty and sundry costs included, far beyond the people's-car brief.
The Suzuki agreements - technology transfer, supply of completely knocked-down units and components for ten years, and the joint venture itself - were signed on 2 October 1982.
The partners had only fourteen months to roll out a small car, per Business Standard's history.
Indira Gandhi handpicked the leadership: Sumant Moolgaokar, Telco's legendary chairman, as non-executive chairman, and V.
Krishnamurthy, the man who had turned around BHEL, as vice chairman, per Forbes India's retelling.
In December 1983, on time against the fourteen-month brief, the first Maruti 800 rolled out - a 796 cc hatchback, per Forbes India's retelling.
The first car went to Harpal Singh, an Indian Airlines employee, per Business Standard's history.
The market it entered barely existed.
When Maruti 800 production began, the entire Indian car market was under 70,000 cars a year, per Suzuki's milestone release.
The Ambassador and the Premier Padmini had defined Indian motoring for a generation; the 800 redefined it in one product cycle.
The scale followed the small car, not the other way round.
The Omni, the Gypsy, the Wagon R, the Alto and the Swift arrived in line with Indian road conditions and consumer demand, per Suzuki's milestone release.
On 15 March 2011 - twenty-seven years and three months after production began - the company built its ten-millionth car, per Suzuki's milestone release.
By then the market around it had passed 3 million cars a year, up from under 70,000 when it started.
Two plants near Delhi, Gurgaon and Manesar, carried a combined annual capacity of 1.2 million cars by 2011, per Suzuki's milestone release.
The company India had doubted had become the machine that made India a car-owning country - by 2014 it was turning out one car every twelve seconds, per Forbes India's retelling.
The ownership travelled the opposite way to the founding.
Maruti became a subsidiary of Suzuki Motor Corporation in 2002, per its FY2025-26 annual report.
In 2003 the government took the company public on the BSE and the NSE; the issue was subscribed 7.82 times, per Business Standard's history.
The state sold more of its holding in 2006 and exited the company entirely in 2007.

As of 31 March 2026, Suzuki Motor Corporation held 58.53% of the equity, per its FY2025-26 annual report - the Indian operation is now the parent's largest subsidiary by production volume and sales, the same report says.
The build story has a chapter the company does not get to skip.
Three labour strikes between June and October 2011 had already rocked the new Manesar plant and crippled production, per Business Standard's history.
Then, on the evening of 18 July 2012, mob violence and arson swept the factory.

Nearly a hundred executives, managers and supervisors were attacked and hospitalised, and Awanish Kumar Dev, the plant's general manager for human resources, was burnt to death, per Maruti's own statement.
The New York Times reported at the time that his lower limbs were fractured at multiple points and that the fire made the body slow to identify; more than seventy workers and executives were injured.
Maruti declared a lockout at the plant.
It remains among the worst episodes of labour violence in Indian corporate history - the cost, in one night, of a labour model that had been fraying for a year.

The Maruti 800 itself is gone: after more than thirty years and almost three million sold worldwide, the company stopped making it, the announcement coming in the week of 7 February 2014 - stricter emission standards and declining sales had made the decision for it, per the New York Times' India blog.
The company the 800 built is not gone.

On 4 June 2018, Suzuki's accumulated production in India crossed twenty million cars - the second country after Japan to reach the milestone, and the fastest: thirty-four years and five months, against forty-five years and nine months in Japan, per Suzuki's release.
The twenty-millionth car was a Swift, built at Suzuki's own Gujarat plant; the Alto was the most-built model, about 3.17 million of them.

And the present tense is still expanding: per its FY2025-26 annual report, FY2025-26 was the company's highest-ever sales year, above two million units for the third year running - the first Indian passenger-vehicle maker to achieve it - with commercial production begun at the new Kharkhoda plant and capacity expanded at Hansalpur.
It is also the country's largest exporter of passenger vehicles.
End where it began: at a signing table on 2 October 1982, with a doubted brief, fourteen months, and a decision to build a small car at a small price for a market that did not yet exist.
The country chose it back.
The first in line was an Indian Airlines employee named Harpal Singh - and forty-three Decembers later, the line has not ended.
